prompt: Why can't prompt injection be solved the way SQL injection is (structural separation of code and data)?

options.text: To an LLM, instructions and data are the same thing: tokens in context; there is no structural channel that keeps them apart
Because LLMs don't process text
Because injection only affects databases
It can: parameterized prompts fully solve it

explanation: Parameterized queries work because SQL has separate structure and data channels. A context window has one channel; any text the model reads can attempt to steer it.

prompt: Indirect prompt injection is especially dangerous because…

options.text: …the malicious instructions hide in third-party content the model reads on a trusted user's behalf: the user is innocent, the document is the attacker
…it requires physical access to the server
…it only works on open-source models
…it needs the user's password

explanation: The payload rides in emails, webpages, PDFs, or retrieved chunks. Your legitimate user triggers it unknowingly, which is why retrieved content and tool results are untrusted input.

prompt: Why is 'train a classifier to detect malicious instructions' an insufficient primary defense?

options.text: Injections can be paraphrased, encoded, translated, or split across chunks: a classifier chases yesterday's phrasings in an unwinnable arms race
Classifiers are too expensive to run
It works perfectly and is sufficient
Detection is illegal

explanation: Filtering raises attacker cost but never reaches 100%. Real boundaries constrain what a (sometimes-fooled) model can DO, not what it's told.

prompt: Least privilege stops many injection attacks without detecting them because…

options.text: …a capability that doesn't exist can't be abused, whatever the model was tricked into wanting: the defense is unconditional across all phrasings and future variants
…it makes the model ignore instructions
…it encrypts the untrusted content
…it slows the model down

explanation: Absence of capability is a real boundary; obedience to the injection has nothing to execute. This is why it works where filtering only hopes.

prompt: The 'lethal trifecta' that makes an AI system seriously dangerous is…

options.text: Access to private data + exposure to untrusted content + ability to communicate/act externally
Large model + long context + high temperature
Slow responses + high cost + poor UX
Public data + trusted content + read-only tools

explanation: Injection enters via untrusted content, harvests private data, and exfiltrates via external egress. Break any leg (often by gating or allowlisting egress) and the classic attack collapses.

prompt: Executing model-generated code with eval() (or interpolating model output into SQL) is dangerous because…

options.text: …model output is untrusted input to the next system; combined with injection, a poisoned input becomes arbitrary code/query execution
…eval() is deprecated syntax
…it only fails when the user is malicious
…model output is always safe to execute

explanation: 'Model output → dangerous sink' is the insecure-output-handling failure. Treat model output with the same suspicion as user input: validate, sandbox, or don't execute.

prompt: The core mindset of defense in depth is…

options.text: …assume each layer sometimes fails, and stack independent layers so no single failure is catastrophic
…make one layer (the injection filter) perfect
…rely on the model's good judgment
…add layers only after an incident

explanation: Independent controls multiply: input boundaries, least privilege, approval gates, output validation, and monitoring each catch what the others miss.

prompt: A ~92%-effective injection classifier is proposed as sufficient to ship an agent with database-write tools. Correct response:

options.text: Ship only with independent layers beneath it (least privilege on writes, approval gates, output validation, rate limits) so the residual ~8% can't cause serious harm
Ship it; 92% is a passing grade
Remove the classifier and trust the model
Raise it to 95% and ship

explanation: No single probabilistic control is enough for consequential capabilities. The layers below assume the filter fails, because it will.

prompt: Per-user document access in RAG must be enforced by…

options.text: …filtering at retrieval time in code, so unauthorized chunks never enter the context
…instructing the model to only discuss the user's own data
…a disclaimer in the UI
…a larger model that respects boundaries

explanation: Anything placed in context can surface in output; a prompt is not a security control. Access control is code that runs before the prompt is built: critical in multi-tenant systems.

prompt: Sending each customer's entire CRM record in every prompt violates which principle, and why does it matter?

options.text: Data minimization: surplus sensitive fields multiply breach impact across provider transfer and logs, and exceed the lawful-basis/purpose limits of most privacy regimes
It doesn't matter; more context is always better
It only affects latency
Data maximization: always send everything

explanation: Send only what the task needs. Every extra field is copied into transfers and traces, enlarging the blast radius of any leak, and minimization is a legal expectation, not just hygiene.

prompt: A regulator asks why the system made a specific decision last quarter. What makes an accountable answer possible?

options.text: Versioned prompts/models/data plus decision logs that let you reconstruct the exact inputs, sources, config, and responsible owner
Explaining that the model is a black box
Re-running today's system and assuming parity
Citing the provider's terms of service

explanation: Governance requires reconstruction and a named human owner. 'The AI decided' is not accountable; a reproducible logged record is.

prompt: A lightweight AI threat model should include which steps? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enumerate assets: sensitive data, tools, and irreversible actions
Enumerate entry points where untrusted content enters (inputs, RAG corpus, tool results, uploads)
Trace attack paths to the highest-blast-radius reachable action, then red-team them
Assume the system is safe because it uses a reputable model

explanation: Assets, entry points, attack paths, and actual red-teaming (with findings added to the eval suite). Model reputation is not a threat model.

prompt: Tool results (API responses, file contents, web pages fetched by an agent) must be treated as untrusted because…

options.text: …they carry third-party content into the context: a fetched webpage or poisoned database field is an indirect injection vector exactly like an uploaded document
…APIs are usually broken
…tools run on slower servers
…they aren't; tools are inside the trust boundary

explanation: The injection surface is 'any text the model reads', not 'any text the user types'. Retrieved chunks, tool outputs, and documents all qualify.

prompt: Approval fatigue (humans rubber-stamping gates) is best mitigated by…

options.text: …gating fewer, higher-stakes actions with rich context per request: reserving human attention for decisions that matter instead of diluting it across everything
…adding more approval steps
…removing approvals entirely
…punishing fast approvers

explanation: Attention is a budget. A gate on everything is a gate on nothing; calibrated scope plus decision-ready context keeps the human check real.

prompt: Data minimization applies to traces and logs by…

options.text: …redacting secrets and unneeded personal data at capture and setting retention limits: the observability store is part of the attack surface
…logging everything forever for completeness
…disabling logging entirely
…encrypting logs and never rotating keys

explanation: You cannot leak what you didn't keep. Minimization is a design constraint on every copy (prompts, traces, backups) not just the primary database.

prompt: Model output flowing into a SQL query, shell command, or HTML page is dangerous because…

options.text: …output is untrusted input to the next system: injection through the model becomes SQL injection, command injection, or XSS at the sink; parameterize, sandbox, or sanitize there
…models format SQL badly
…it's slow
…it isn't; model output is safe by construction

explanation: The sink defines the risk. Every classical injection defense applies at the boundary where model text meets an interpreter.

prompt: Before sending regulated data to a model API, you must verify the provider's…

options.text: …the provider's data-handling terms for retention, training use, residency, and available zero-retention or enterprise controls
…logo quality
…model parameter count
…nothing; APIs are all equivalent

explanation: Where data flows is a compliance question answered by the DPA and terms. For hard residency constraints, Module 17's self-hosting is the alternative.

prompt: Ranking risks by 'blast radius' means prioritizing…

options.text: …the worst reachable consequence (irreversible actions, mass data exposure) over the most likely small one: the send-all-contacts email outranks a typo in a summary
…the most frequent bug
…whatever was in the news
…alphabetical order

explanation: Threat models sort by consequence × reachability. The highest-blast-radius action gets the strongest walls (privilege, gates) first.

prompt: Red-team findings become durable protection when…

options.text: …each successful attack is added to the eval suite as a permanent regression case: defeated once means detected forever
…they're documented in a slide deck
…the red team is congratulated
…the report is marked confidential

explanation: The failure-museum loop applies to security: attacks that once worked become automated tests that gate every future release.

prompt: Delimiting untrusted text (e.g., <document>…</document>) is necessary but insufficient because…

options.text: …it's hygiene that helps the model separate data from instructions, but a determined injection can still steer the model: real boundaries constrain capabilities, not text
…XML tags cost too many tokens
…models can't see tags
…it is fully sufficient on its own

explanation: Layer one of defense in depth, never the whole defense. Least privilege and gated actions hold when the delimiter doesn't.
